title: The Wind That Shakes the Barley
full_review:
Winner of the top prize at last year's Cannes Film Festival, "The Wind That Shakes the Barley" (IFC) is a powerful war drama about two brothers determined to end British rule over Ireland in the early 1920s.

Although demonstrably on the side of the Irish freedom fighters, director Ken Loach vividly exposes the pitfalls of violence by showing how cycles of reprisal tear apart both the country and the siblings.

Damien (Cillian Murphy) is a medical doctor poised to emigrate when a close friend is beaten to death by British soldiers. (The title comes from a ballad sung at the young man's wake.) He decides to stay and battle alongside his brother, Teddy (Padraic Delaney), leader of their local guerrilla army cell.

Over time, their motivations for ousting the British and gaining independence diverge. Damien grows increasingly ideological, and ardent rebel Teddy comes to represent the law and order establishment.

Aided by the landed aristocracy, the British are villainous yet do not have a monopoly on savagery; the brutal violence perpetrated by both sides is never glamorized.

The narrative, beautifully realized from a production standpoint, has been pared down to its essentials and has the universal, inexorable qualities of a tragic fable.

According to Loach and screenwriter Paul Laverty, the basis of the centuries-old conflict is primarily economic and they champion socialism without ignoring any historical or moral complexity.

Religion is not a major factor. (Worth noting: The action takes place in the South prior to the partitioning of the North, where sectarian strife occurred in the latter decades of the 20th century.) There's one anti-Catholic slur: Ireland is referred to as a "priest-infested backwater." Two Catholic clerics appear as characters. The first hears confession and blesses members of the IRA cell before they carry out a mission with a high body count. The second urges his congregation to honor the 1921 cease-fire and treaty negotiations, and is, despite an officious demeanor, a voice of peace and reason.

The film contains pervasive rough and crude language, including one anti-Catholic slur, extensive wartime violence, including multiple shootings and executions, a torture scene, and an unmarried man and woman kiss briefly prior to an implied encounter. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. Not rated by the Motion Picture Association of America.
